transcription.tex: Differential equations relate variables and their derivatives. A first-order equation contains a first derivative but no higher derivatives.
The rate of temperature loss is proportional to the temperature above the surroundings. Here \(T\) is the excess temperature.
The population changes at a rate proportional to \(P(1-P/M)\), with limiting population \(M\) (Verhulst–Pearl model).
GDP \(x\) grows at a rate proportional to its current value.
Applications in physics and engineering include radioactive decay, mixing fluids, cooling materials and bodies falling against resistance.

transcription.tex: Separation of variables applies when the right-hand side is a product of one function of \(x\) and one of \(y\):\[\frac{dy}{dx}=f(x)g(y).\]For \(g(y)\ne0\), divide through:\[\frac1{g(y)}\frac{dy}{dx}=f(x).\]
Multiply by \(dx\) and integrate:\[\int\frac1{g(y)}\,dy=\int f(x)\,dx.\]Include an arbitrary integration constant. Check separately for constant solutions satisfying \(g(y)=0\).

transcription.tex: Why is it called the general solution?
The arbitrary constant gives a family of solutions.
\[\int y\,dy=\int-x\,dx\]\[\tfrac12y^2=-\tfrac12x^2+C\]\[x^2+y^2=2C=r^2.\]The family of circles satisfies the equation wherever \(y\ne0\).

transcription.tex: \[\frac{dy}{dx}=x(y+1)\]\[\int\frac1{y+1}\,dy=\int x\,dx\]\[\ln|y+1|=\tfrac12x^2+C\]\[|y+1|=e^{x^2/2+C}=e^{x^2/2}e^C\]\[y+1=Ae^{x^2/2}.\]Absorb the sign into real \(A\). Including \(A=0\) restores the equilibrium solution \(y=-1\).

\[\int\frac1y\,dy=\int-\frac1x\,dx\]\[\ln|y|=-\ln|x|+C\]\[\ln|x|+\ln|y|=C\]\[\ln|xy|=C\Rightarrow |xy|=e^C\]\[y=\frac A x,\quad A\in\mathbb R.\]This is a family of rectangular hyperbolas; \(A=0\) also gives a solution.

The coefficient of \(y^{\prime}\) becomes the factor multiplying \(y\) inside the derivative.

transcription.tex: For \(y^{\prime}+Py=Q\), suppose \(f(x)\) is an integrating factor. Multiply through:\[fy^{\prime}+fPy=fQ.\]To use reverse product rule, the left side must equal \(fy^{\prime}+f^{\prime}y\).
Choose \(f>0\), divide and integrate:\[\int\frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\int P\,dx\]\[\ln f(x)=\int P\,dx.\]
\[f(x)=e^{\int P\,dx}.\]A non-zero constant multiplier does not affect the method.

transcription.tex: Solve \(\cos x\,y^{\prime}+2y\sin x=\cos^4x\). What should we do first?
1. Divide by \(\cos x\), on intervals where it is non-zero:\[y^{\prime}+2y\tan x=\cos^3x.\]
3. Multiply through:\[\sec^2x\,y^{\prime}+2y\sec^2x\tan x=\cos x\]\[\frac d{dx}(y\sec^2x)=\cos x.\]You can go straight to this derivative, but remember to multiply the right side by the factor too.

transcription.tex: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}+2xy=\mathrm e^{-x^2}$

\(\text{Integrating factor}=\mathrm e^{\int P(x)\,\mathrm dx}=\mathrm e^{\int2x\,\mathrm dx}=\mathrm e^{x^2}\)\par \(\mathrm e^{x^2}\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}+2x\mathrm e^{x^2}y=1\)\par \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}(y\mathrm e^{x^2})=1\)\par \(y\mathrm e^{x^2}=\int1\,\mathrm dx=x+c\)\par \(y=\frac{x+c}{\mathrm e^{x^2}}=x\mathrm e^{-x^2}+c\mathrm e^{-x^2}\)
\(y=\frac{x+c}{\mathrm e^{x^2}}\)\par As $x\to\infty$, $\mathrm e^{x^2}$ grows faster than $x+c$, so $y\to0$.

transcription.tex: Find $y$ in terms of $x$ given that $x\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}+2y=\mathrm e^x$ and that $y=1$ when $x=1$.

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}+\frac2x y=\frac{\mathrm e^x}{x},\qquad \text{Integrating factor}=\mathrm e^{\int(2/x)\,\mathrm dx}=\mathrm e^{2\ln x}=\mathrm e^{\ln x^2}=x^2\)\par \(x^2\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}+2xy=x\mathrm e^x\quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}(x^2y)=x\mathrm e^x\)\par \(x^2y=\int x\mathrm e^x\,\mathrm dx=x\mathrm e^x-\int \mathrm e^x\,\mathrm dx=x\mathrm e^x-\mathrm e^x+c\)\par \(y=\frac{\mathrm e^x}{x}-\frac{\mathrm e^x}{x^2}+\frac{c}{x^2}\)\par \(y(1)=1\quad\Rightarrow\quad1=\mathrm e-\mathrm e+c\quad\Rightarrow\quad c=1\)\par \(y=\frac{\mathrm e^x}{x}-\frac{\mathrm e^x}{x^2}+\frac1{x^2}\)

transcription.tex: Solve the differential equation, giving $y$ in terms of $x$, where $x^3\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}-x^2y=1$ and $y=1$ at $x=1$.

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}-\frac1xy=\frac1{x^3},\qquad \text{Integrating factor}=\mathrm e^{-\int(1/x)\,\mathrm dx}=\mathrm e^{-\ln x}=\mathrm e^{\ln(1/x)}=\frac1x\)\par \(\frac1x \frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}-\frac1{x^2}y=\frac1{x^4}\quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\left(\frac yx\right)=\frac1{x^4}\)\par \(\frac yx=\int\frac1{x^4}\,\mathrm dx=\int x^{-4}\,\mathrm dx=-\frac13x^{-3}+c\)\par \(y=-\frac13 x^{-2}+cx=-\frac1{3x^2}+cx\)\par \(y(1)=1\quad\Rightarrow\quad1=-\frac13+c\quad\Rightarrow\quad c=\frac43\)\par \(y=-\frac1{3x^2}+\frac{4x}{3}\)

transcription.tex: Find the general solution to the differential equation\par $\left(x+\frac1x\right)\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}+2y=2(x^2+1)^2$\par giving $y$ in terms of $x$.

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}+\frac2{x+1/x}y=\frac{2(x^2+1)^2}{x+1/x}\quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}+\frac{2x}{x^2+1}y=2x(x^2+1)\)\par \(\text{Integrating factor}=\mathrm e^{\int\frac{2x}{x^2+1}\,\mathrm dx}=\mathrm e^{\ln(x^2+1)}=x^2+1\)\par \((x^2+1)\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}+2xy=2x(x^2+1)^2\quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}((x^2+1)y)=2x(x^2+1)^2\)\par \(y(x^2+1)=\int2x(x^2+1)^2\,\mathrm dx=\frac13(x^2+1)^3+c\)\par \(y=\frac13(x^2+1)^2+\frac{c}{x^2+1}\)

transcription.tex: Find the general solution to the differential equation\par $\cos x\,\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}+y=1,\quad-\frac\pi2<x<\frac\pi2$

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}+y\sec x=\sec x,\qquad\int\sec x\,\mathrm dx=\ln(\sec x+\tan x)+c\)\par \(\text{Integrating factor}=\mathrm e^{\int\sec x\,\mathrm dx}=\mathrm e^{\ln(\sec x+\tan x)}=\sec x+\tan x\)\par \((\sec x+\tan x)\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}+(\sec^2 x+\sec x\tan x)y=\sec^2 x+\sec x\tan x\)\par \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}((\sec x+\tan x)y)=\sec^2 x+\sec x\tan x\)\par \((\sec x+\tan x)y=\int(\sec^2 x+\sec x\tan x)\,\mathrm dx=\tan x+\sec x+c\)\par \(y=1+\frac{c}{\sec x+\tan x}\)

transcription.tex: Find the general solution to the differential equation\par $\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=x\sqrt{y^2-4}$
Problem-solving   You can use the substitution $y=2\cosh u$ to integrate $\frac1{\sqrt{y^2-4}}$   ← Section 6.5

\(\frac1{\sqrt{y^2-4}}\,\mathrm dy=x\,\mathrm dx,\qquad y=2\cosh u\ (u>0),\quad\mathrm dy=2\sinh u\,\mathrm du\)\par \(\int\frac{\,\mathrm dy}{\sqrt{y^2-4}}=\int\frac{2\sinh u}{\sqrt{4\cosh^2u-4}}\,\mathrm du=\int\frac{2\sinh u}{2\sinh u}\,\mathrm du=\int1\,\mathrm du\)\par \(=u+c=\operatorname{arcosh}(y/2)+c\)\par \(\operatorname{arcosh}(y/2)=\frac{x^2}{2}+c\quad\Rightarrow\quad y=2\cosh\left(\frac{x^2}{2}+c\right),\quad\frac{x^2}{2}+c\ge0\)\par On the negative branch $y=-2\cosh(c-x^2/2)$ where $c-x^2/2\ge0$. The constant solutions are $y=\pm2$.

transcription.tex: Find the general solution to the differential equation\par $\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=y\cosh x$
Find the particular solution which satisfies the condition that $y=\mathrm e$ when $x=0$.

\(\frac1y\,\mathrm dy=\cosh x\,\mathrm dx\quad\Rightarrow\quad\ln|y|=\sinh x+c\)\par \(y=\mathrm e^{\sinh x+c}\quad(y>0)\)\par Allowing either sign and $y=0$ gives $y=C\mathrm e^{\sinh x}$ for every real $C$.
\(\mathrm e=\mathrm e^{\sinh0+c}=\mathrm e^c\quad\Rightarrow\quad c=1\)\par \(y=\mathrm e^{\sinh x+1}\)

transcription.tex: Find the general solution to the differential equation\par $\cos x\,\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}+y\sin x=1$

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}+y\tan x=\sec x,\qquad \text{Integrating factor}=\mathrm e^{\int\tan x\,\mathrm dx}=\mathrm e^{\ln|\sec x|}\)\par On each interval with $\cos x\ne0$, take $\sec x$ as the integrating factor.\par \(\sec x\,\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}+y\sec x\tan x=\sec^2x\quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}(y\sec x)=\sec^2x\)\par \(y\sec x=\int\sec^2x\,\mathrm dx=\tan x+c\)\par \(y=\sin x+c\cos x\)

transcription.tex: Find the particular solution such that $y=3$ when $x=\pi$.
Show that the points $\left(\frac\pi2,1\right)$ and $\left(\frac{3\pi}2,-1\right)$ lie on all possible solution curves.

\(x=\frac\pi2:\quad y=\sin\frac\pi2+c\cos\frac\pi2=1+c\times0=1\)\par \(x=\frac{3\pi}2:\quad y=\sin\frac{3\pi}2+c\cos\frac{3\pi}2=-1+c\times0=-1\)\par These values hold for every $c$, so both points lie on every solution curve.

transcription.tex: Find a general solution to the equation $a\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}+by=0$ in terms of $a$ and $b$.

\(a\ne0:\quad \frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}+\frac ba y=0,\qquad \text{Integrating factor}=\mathrm e^{\int (b/a)\,\mathrm dx}=\mathrm e^{bx/a}\)\par \(\mathrm e^{bx/a}\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}+\frac ba \mathrm e^{bx/a}y=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}(\mathrm e^{bx/a}y)=0\)\par \(\mathrm e^{bx/a}y=c\quad\Rightarrow\quad y=c\mathrm e^{-bx/a}\)\par If $a=0$ and $b\ne0$, $y=0$. If $a=b=0$, any differentiable $y$ satisfies the equation.

transcription.tex: If \(m\) is a root of \(am^2+bm+c=0\), then \(Ae^{mx}\) solves \(ay^{\prime\prime}+by^{\prime}+cy=0\).\par For distinct real roots \(\alpha,\beta\):\[y=Ae^{\alpha x}+Be^{\beta x}.\]Here \(A,B\) are arbitrary constants.\par A zero right-hand side makes the equation homogeneous.

transcription.tex: For two equal roots \(\alpha\), where \(b^2-4ac=0\):\[y=(A+Bx)e^{\alpha x}.\]Show that \((A+Bx)e^{3x}\) satisfies\[y^{\prime\prime}-6y^{\prime}+9y=0.\]The auxiliary equation is \((m-3)^2=0\).

Why not \(Ae^{\alpha x}+Be^{\alpha x}\)? It combines to just one arbitrary constant. The extra \(x\) gives an independent solution, analogous to the distinct terms \(A/x+B/x^2\) used for repeated partial-fraction factors.

transcription.tex: Given the differential equation $\frac{\mathrm d^2x}{\mathrm dt^2}+2k\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}+9x=0$, where $k$ is a real constant,
find the general solution to the differential equation in each of the following cases:

\(m^2+2km+9=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad m=\frac{-2k\pm\sqrt{4k^2-36}}2=-k\pm\sqrt{k^2-9}\)\par The two roots are real and distinct.\par \(x=A\mathrm e^{(-k+\sqrt{k^2-9})t}+B\mathrm e^{(-k-\sqrt{k^2-9})t}\)

\(m^2+2km+9=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad m=\frac{-2k\pm\sqrt{4k^2-36}}2=-k\pm\sqrt{k^2-9}\)\par The two roots are complex conjugates, $-k\pm\mathrm i\sqrt{9-k^2}$.\par \(x=\mathrm e^{-kt}\left(A\cos\left(\sqrt{9-k^2}\,t\right)+B\sin\left(\sqrt{9-k^2}\,t\right)\right)\)
\(m^2+2km+9=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad m=\frac{-2k\pm\sqrt{4k^2-36}}2=-k\pm\sqrt{k^2-9}\)\par The auxiliary equation has the repeated root $-k$.\par \(x=(A+Bt)\mathrm e^{-kt}\)

transcription.tex: Given the differential equation $\frac{\mathrm d^2x}{\mathrm dt^2}+2k\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}+9x=0$, where $k$ is a real constant,\par \textbf{b} In the case where $k=2$,
Use part a ii with $k=2$. Then $\sqrt{9-k^2}=\sqrt{9-4}=\sqrt5$.\par \(x=\mathrm e^{-2t}\left(A\cos(\sqrt5\,t)+B\sin(\sqrt5\,t)\right)\)
As $t\to\infty$, $\mathrm e^{-2t}\to0$. The trigonometric functions are bounded, so $x\to0$.

transcription.tex: What if the right-hand side is a function of \(x\)?\[ay^{\prime\prime}+by^{\prime}+cy=f(x).\]This is non-homogeneous when \(f\) is not identically zero.\par First solve the homogeneous equation:\[ay^{\prime\prime}+by^{\prime}+cy=0.\]Its general solution is the complementary function (CF).

Next find one solution of\[ay^{\prime\prime}+by^{\prime}+cy=f(x)\]by choosing an appropriate trial function and comparing coefficients. This is the particular integral (PI).\[y=\mathrm{CF}+\mathrm{PI}.\]The differential operator gives zero for the CF and \(f(x)\) for the PI; adding gives \(f(x)\).
